steps: This video shows how an agent can use a secret A P I key without the model ever seeing it. Billing clerk forty-seven signs in through single sign-on with billing scope and asks the agent server about customer C seventy-seven.
First, the wrong way. The server puts the C R M key straight into the system prompt sent to Claude. Now the key sits in context, visible in every trace, and can leak through logs or prompt injection.
Now the better design. The server sends Claude only the question and the tool definitions, with no secret in context. Claude replies with a tool request: lookup customer, C seventy-seven.
When the tool runs, the server's handler fetches the C R M A P I key from Key Vault. It is used in the request header and then discarded, all on the server side.

The C R M call also carries the clerk's billing-scoped token, so role-based access control runs before any data returns. Only billing documents come back, because V I P notes need V I P support access.
The server sends Claude the tool result, and Claude writes the billing answer for C seventy-seven. Claude never held the key at any point.

The clerk receives a billing-only answer, and the server's audit log records that clerk forty-seven viewed customer C seventy-seven. Takeaway: secrets stay in the vault and the handler, never in model context. The full walkthrough is in the Gennoor Claude certification course.
